Blunt take first: **real photos make or break this.** Stock photos and AI-generated images are what make optical sites look like slop. Spend one afternoon shooting the actual frames on a plain surface in daylight, plus the shop front. Everything below assumes you do that.

## Direction

**Stack:** Next.js (App Router) + TypeScript + Tailwind. Products live in one typed `products.ts` file now. When ecommerce comes later, you swap that file for a DB or API and nothing else changes.

**Audience reality:** Almost all traffic will be phones on mediocre mobile data. Optimize images hard, keep the WhatsApp button always reachable, and consider English + Urdu later.

**Look (the anti-slop part):**
- Warm off-white background, near-black text, one accent (deep tortoiseshell brown, bottle green, or burgundy). No purple/blue gradients.
- Type pairing: a serif display font (Fraunces or Cormorant Garamond) with a clean sans (DM Sans or Manrope). Not Inter everywhere.
- Eyewear-specific details: circular lens-shaped image masks, thin hairline dividers, big product photos with lots of whitespace.
- No glassmorphism, no emoji icons, no "Welcome to our website" copy, no fake testimonials, no lorem ipsum.

**Pages:**
1. Home: hero, featured frames, categories, why Mehar for Eyes, shop location and hours, sticky WhatsApp CTA
2. Collection: filter by category (men / women / kids / sunglasses / lenses), gender, frame shape
3. Product detail: gallery, details, "Order on WhatsApp" button with a prefilled message
4. About / Visit us: story, address, map, hours, eye-test info if offered

Good plan, but it changes the architecture. `products.ts` is now only a dev stub. Products and images must live in a database + storage, and the site reads from there.

**Google images:** fine as placeholders while building. Do not launch with them. They're copyrighted, they look inconsistent, and they make the site look like every other cheap optical site. Treat the launch gate as: father uploads real photos first.

## Recommended stack

**Next.js + Supabase** (Postgres + Auth + Storage in one). Fastest path to a working admin, and ecommerce can be added on the same DB later.

- Public site: reads products from Supabase (server components, cached/revalidated).
- `/admin`: login-protected dashboard.
- Images: Supabase Storage bucket, public read, admin-only write.

You could do this with your Go backend, but it means building auth, upload handling, and image resizing yourself. Not worth it for this project.

## Admin must be built for your father, not for you
- Phone-first. He will upload straight from the phone camera.
- Big buttons, minimal fields, English labels now (Urdu labels optional later).
- Auto-resize and compress on upload, so 8MB phone photos don't kill mobile load times.
- One "in stock / out of stock" toggle per product.

## Update the Cursor rules first
In `.cursor/rules/mehar.mdc`, replace the products rule with:

```
- Products come only from the Supabase `products` table via /lib/products.ts data functions. UI never hardcodes product info. /data/products.ts is a dev seed only, to be deleted before launch.
- Images are stored in Supabase Storage bucket `product-images`. Always render through next/image.
- Admin routes live under /app/admin and must be server-side protected. Never trust client checks.
```

(4) /lib/supabase/server.ts and client.ts using @supabase/ssr. (5) a seed script that inserts my 6 placeholder products. Return full files and the exact commands to run.

**Prompt B: swap the site to the DB**

```
Replace all reads from /data/products.ts with data functions in /lib/products.ts (getProducts with filters, getProductBySlug, getFeatured, getRelated) querying Supabase. Add Supabase email/password auth for /admin. Create /admin/login. Protect all /admin routes with middleware AND server-side session checks. Only allow users whose email matches env ADMIN_EMAIL. No public signup route. Logged-out users redirect to /admin/login. Return full files.
```

```
Build /admin: a mobile-first product list (thumbnail, name, category, in-stock toggle, featured toggle, edit and delete buttons with confirm dialog). Build /admin/products/new and /admin/products/[id]/edit with one form: name, brand, category (select), gender (select), frame shape (select), material, color, price (optional), description, in stock, featured. Use server actions with zod validation. Auto-generate slug from name, ensure uniqueness. Revalidate public pages after every save. Big touch-friendly inputs, plain labels, clear success and error messages. No UI library.
```

i am confused, what is supabase, never heard of it, which tech stack we are uszing

---

# claude response

Fair, I dropped it on you without explaining.

## What Supabase is
A ready-made backend you rent instead of building. It gives you three things in one place:

1. **Database** (Postgres): stores products, names, prices, categories.
2. **Auth**: login system for your father's admin dashboard.
3. **Storage**: where uploaded photos live (like a folder on the internet with a URL for each image).

Think of it as "the Go backend + database + file upload server" that you'd otherwise write and host yourself. It has a free tier that is more than enough for this site.

## The full stack

| Part | Tech | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Website + admin UI | Next.js + TypeScript + Tailwind | Public pages and `/admin` pages, one project |
| Data + login + images | Supabase | Products table, admin login, photo storage |
| Hosting | Vercel | Deploys the Next.js app from GitHub |
| Orders | WhatsApp `wa.me` links | No backend needed for orders |

Flow: father logs into `/admin` → uploads photos and product details → saved in Supabase → public site reads from Supabase and shows them.

## Your other option (uses your Go skills)
- Next.js frontend (same)
- Go API + Postgres on a VPS
- Images on S3 or Cloudinary
- You write auth, upload endpoints, image resizing, deployment, backups

This is more work, more to maintain, more that can break. Choose it only if you want full control or already have a VPS you want to use.

## My recommendation
Supabase. Reason: this is a showcase site, and your time is better spent on design and the admin UX than on rebuilding auth and file uploads. If ecommerce comes later, Supabase's Postgres still works; you can add a Go service next to it if needed.

Tell me which one, and I'll give you the exact Cursor prompts for that path. If Supabase, the prompts A-F from my last message are ready to use as written. If Go, I'll rewrite them.

# you asked

message time: 2026-10-23 23:28:45

so i have to buy supabase?

---

# claude response

No. Supabase has a free plan, and for this project it is enough to start.

The free tier gives you 500 MB of database storage, 50,000 monthly active users, 5 GB of egress, 500 MB of file storage, and up to 2 active projects. One source lists 1 GB of file storage instead, so check supabase.com/pricing when you sign up. Either way, it covers a catalog of a few hundred products with compressed photos. That's why prompt E resizes images to WebP before upload.

## The catch you need to know
Free projects auto-pause after one week of inactivity. If nobody opens the site or admin for 7 days, the database goes to sleep and the public site shows errors or empty pages until you wake it manually in the dashboard. For a shop's public site, that is a real problem.

Fixes:
1. **Free workaround:** a scheduled ping (Vercel cron or a GitHub Action) that hits a cheap query once a day. This keeps it active. It works, but it's a hack.
2. **Proper fix:** the Pro plan. It costs $25/month. Pro projects stay running. Upgrade when the site goes live and real customers use it.

## Cost summary for this project

| Part | Cost |
|---|---|
| Supabase (dev + early launch) | $0 |
| Vercel hosting (Hobby plan) | $0 (Vercel's terms restrict Hobby to non-commercial use, so for a business site you'll likely need Pro at ~$20/mo; check their pricing page) |
| Domain (.com or .pk) | ~$10-15/year |
| WhatsApp links | $0 |

If you want zero monthly cost and full control, the Go + Postgres on your own VPS route avoids Supabase fees, but you pay with your time and maintenance. For a business site where your father depends on it, I'd still take Supabase Free while building, then pay for Pro at launch.

Next step: create a free account at supabase.com, make a project, and run prompt A from before. Tell me when you hit an error and paste it verbatim.

---

# claude response

You can. I wasn't saying you couldn't. I picked Supabase to save you time, not because the backend is beyond you. For a Go developer, this is a legitimate and arguably better fit.

## Honest tradeoffs

**What you gain:**
- $0 extra if you already have a VPS. No auto-pause, no vendor limits.
- You own the data and the images.
- Ecommerce later (orders, stock, payments like JazzCash/Easypaisa) is natural to extend in Go.
- It matches your strongest skill.

**What you take on:**
- Auth, upload handling, image processing, backups, deploys, and uptime are all yours.
- If the site goes down, your father calls you. Permanently.
- Security mistakes are on you (file upload endpoints are a classic attack surface).

None of it is hard for you. It's maintenance, not difficulty. If you accept being the sysadmin for this site, go Go.

## Stack

| Part | Tech |
|---|---|
| Public site + admin UI | Next.js + TypeScript + Tailwind |
| API | Go (chi router) + pgx + sqlc |
| DB | Postgres |
| Migrations | golang-migrate |
| Images | Stored on VPS disk (or Cloudflare R2), served via Cloudflare CDN |
| Auth | Single admin, argon2 password hash, httpOnly session cookie |
| Deploy | Docker Compose + Caddy (auto HTTPS) |

Put **Cloudflare** (free plan) in front of the domain. It caches images at edge nodes, which helps on weak Pakistani mobile connections.

## Prompts

**Update `.cursor/rules/mehar.mdc`, replace the data rule with:**

```
- Backend is a separate Go service in /backend (chi, pgx, sqlc, golang-migrate, Postgres). Frontend never talks to the DB directly, only to the Go API.
- Public pages fetch from the API server-side in Next.js with revalidation. Admin pages call the API with the session cookie.
- Images are stored on disk under /data/uploads and served by Caddy at /uploads/*. DB stores only the relative path.
- Go rules: no global state, context passed everywhere, errors wrapped, all inputs validated, parameterized queries only via sqlc. Give full files, not snippets.
```

**Prompt A: backend foundation + schema**

```
Create /backend as a Go 1.22+ module. Structure: cmd/api/main.go, internal/{config,db,http,auth,products,images}. Use chi, pgx/v5, sqlc, golang-migrate. Write migrations for: products (id uuid pk, slug unique, name, brand, category, gender, frame_shape, material, color, price int nullable, description, in_stock bool default true, featured bool default false, sort_order int, created_at, updated_at), product_images (id uuid, product_id fk on delete cascade, path, alt, position int), admin_sessions (id, token_hash, expires_at). Write sqlc queries and config via env vars. Add docker-compose.yml with postgres and the api. Add /healthz. Return all files and exact commands to run.
```

**Prompt B: admin auth**

```
Implement single-admin auth in Go. Admin email and argon2id password hash come from env (provide a small cmd/hashpw tool to generate the hash). POST /api/admin/login sets an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax session cookie with a random 32-byte token (store only its SHA-256 in admin_sessions, 7 day expiry). POST /api/admin/logout. Middleware protecting all /api/admin/* routes. Add login rate limiting per IP (5 attempts per 15 minutes) and constant-time comparisons. CSRF protection via a double-submit token or Origin header check on mutating requests. Return full files.
```

**Prompt C: product API**

```
Build the products API. Public: GET /api/products (filters: category, gender, frame_shape, featured, q; pagination), GET /api/products/{slug}, GET /api/products/{slug}/related. Admin: POST /api/admin/products, PUT /api/admin/products/{id}, DELETE /api/admin/products/{id}, PATCH /api/admin/products/{id}/stock, PATCH /api/admin/products/{id}/featured. Validate every field, generate unique slug from name, return consistent JSON errors. Add tests for slug generation and validation. Return full files.
```

**Prompt D: image upload (security-critical)**

```
Build image upload in Go: POST /api/admin/products/{id}/images (multipart, up to 8 files, max 5MB each, max 8 images per product). Server-side: sniff real content type with http.DetectContentType (allow only jpeg, png, webp, never trust extension or header), decode and re-encode to strip EXIF and any embedded payload, resize to max 1600px, also generate a 600px thumbnail, save as WebP using libvips via bimg (or kolesa-team/go-webp), name files with uuid, write to /data/uploads/products/{id}/. PUT to reorder images, DELETE to remove (delete files from disk too). Limit request body with http.MaxBytesReader. Return full files and the Dockerfile changes needed for libvips.
```

**Prompt E: frontend**

```
Build the Next.js admin: /admin/login, /admin product list (mobile-first, thumbnail, in-stock toggle, featured toggle, edit, delete with confirm), /admin/products/new and /[id]/edit form with all product fields and multi-image upload (camera and gallery input, client-side resize to WebP before upload, progress, touch reorder, delete). Call the Go API with credentials: 'include'. Protect admin routes in middleware by checking a session probe endpoint. Then switch all public pages to fetch from the Go API server-side with revalidate 60. Remove /data/products.ts. Return full files.
```

**Prompt F: deploy and backups**

```
Write production deployment: docker-compose.prod.yml with caddy, next app, go api, postgres, a volume for /data/uploads. Caddyfile with auto HTTPS, reverse proxy /api to Go, serve /uploads/* statically with long cache headers, security headers. A nightly backup script: pg_dump plus rsync of /data/uploads to a second location, keep 14 days, with cron and restore instructions. Add a GitHub Actions workflow to build and deploy over SSH. Return full files and exact commands.
```

## Warnings
- **Upload endpoint:** the re-encode step in prompt D is not optional. It's what kills malicious files disguised as images.
- **Backups:** test a restore once. An untested backup is not a backup.
- **Cloudflare:** set cache rules for `/uploads/*`. Do not cache `/api/admin/*`.
- **Don't expose Postgres** to the public internet. Docker internal network only.

Where are you hosting? If you already have a VPS at Tawha or elsewhere, tell me the OS and RAM, and I'll adjust the Docker and Caddy setup.

# claude response

Not really, and I wouldn't do it anyway.

**Why I can't check it properly**
- My terminal can only reach a short list of approved sites, so I can't open your IP or port.
- I do have a page-fetch tool that can open a public URL you give me, but it only returns the page's text and HTML. It doesn't show me how the page looks: layout, spacing, colors, mobile view. That's the thing I'd be checking, so screenshots from you work better.

**Why port forwarding is a bad idea**
- It opens a hole from the internet into your PC. The Next.js dev server is not built to face the public, so don't expose it.
- It breaks whenever your IP changes or the PC sleeps.

**Better options**
1. **Screenshots (easiest).** Send me a screenshot of each page, desktop and mobile. This is all I need to give design feedback.
2. **Vercel preview (best for sharing).** Push the project to GitHub, import it on vercel.com, and you get a free public link. Your father or friends can open it on their phones, and you can send me the link too. Remember to add `NEXT_PUBLIC_WHATSAPP_NUMBER` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` in Vercel's environment settings.
3. **Temporary tunnel.** If you only want a quick link to test on your own phone, Cloudflare Tunnel or ngrok gives a temporary public URL without opening your router. Close it when you're done.

For now, do option 1. Send me the product page screenshots when it's built, and we'll move on to the floating WhatsApp button.

```
import type { MetadataRoute } from "next";
import { getProducts } from "@/lib/products";
import { siteConfig } from "@/lib/site";

export default async function sitemap(): Promise<MetadataRoute.Sitemap> {
  const products = await getProducts({});
  const now = new Date();
  const staticPages = ["", "/collection", "/about"].map((path) => ({
    url: siteConfig.url + path,
    lastModified: now,
  }));
  const productPages = products.map((p) => ({
    url: siteConfig.url + "/collection/" + p.slug,
    lastModified: now,
  }));
  return [...staticPages, ...productPages];
}
```

# claude response

Use **Claude Sonnet** for almost everything. Switch to **Claude Opus** only for the hard parts.

- **Gemini 3.8 Flash (Low)**: this is what you have selected now, and it's the weakest and fastest option on the list. "Low" also means it thinks the least. This is most likely why Antigravity feels bad at making things.
- **Claude Sonnet**: best default for this project. Good at following long, exact prompts like the ones I write, and good at not touching files it shouldn't.
- **Claude Opus**: slower and uses more of your quota. Save it for the Go backend, the auth, and the image upload security step, where a mistake costs more.
- **GPT-OSS 120B**: skip it. The notice says Antigravity removes it on November 2, which is tomorrow.
- **Gemini 4 Argon**: shows as unavailable.

I'm a Claude model, so weigh my recommendation accordingly. But Flash on Low is the weakest option in that list, so switching up is a safe move either way.

Before you rely on it, click **View Usage** at the bottom of that menu. The Claude options may have a limit on your plan, and Opus will use it up faster. If Sonnet runs out, fall back to Gemini Flash, but raise its setting from Low to a higher level if the option exists.

Then paste the big prompt I gave you, using Sonnet. If the result is still bad, send me the error or a screenshot.

## Easy way to open mobile view in Chrome
1. Press **F12** to open the developer panel.
2. Press **Ctrl + Shift + M**. This turns on mobile view, so you don't need to find the icon.

If you want to find the icon by hand: it's in the top-left corner of the developer panel (not the browser), a small icon of a phone and tablet overlapping. If the panel is docked at the bottom or right, look at the very first row of that panel.

## If it still doesn't show
Make the browser window narrow instead. Drag the edge of the Chrome window until it is about 400px wide. The site responds to the real width, so it behaves the same as in phone view.

Or open `http://localhost:3000` on your actual phone. Your PC and phone must be on the same Wi-Fi. Find your PC's IP with `ipconfig` in the terminal (look for IPv4 Address, like `192.168.1.5`), then open `http://192.168.1.5:3000` on the phone. If it doesn't load, Windows Firewall may be blocking it, so skip this one.
